analysis.one_liner: Gives many workers twelve weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a new child or serious illness.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House 265-163 and the Senate 71-27, the House accepted the Senate's changes, and the President signed it into law on February 5, 1993 as Public Law 103-3.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires employers with 50 or more employees within 75 miles of a worksite to give eligible workers up to 12 workweeks of unpaid leave during any 12-month period for the birth or adoption of a child, to care for a seriously ill child, spouse, or parent, or for the worker's own serious health condition [S2]. Workers on leave keep their health benefits and have the right to return to the same job or an equivalent one [S2]. It applies the same rights to federal civil service employees and to Senate and House employees [S2]. Enforcement runs through the Department of Labor, with damages for employers who interfere with these rights [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at covered employers who need time off for a birth, adoption, foster placement, a family member's serious illness, or their own serious illness. They keep their jobs and their health insurance while on leave, something federal law had never guaranteed before.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers needing leave for births or illness

how_it_helps.text: Gives eligible workers 12 workweeks of unpaid leave per year for the birth or adoption of a child, care of a seriously ill family member, or their own serious health condition [S2].
Requires employers to maintain health benefits during the leave and to restore the worker to the same or an equivalent position afterward [S2].
Makes it illegal for an employer to interfere with or discriminate against workers exercising these rights, and lets the Labor Department enforce the law with damages and reinstatement [S2].
Extends the same leave rights to federal civil service employees and to employees of the House and Senate [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers, generally private businesses with 50 or more employees nearby, plus government agencies. They must hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, keep paying health premiums for workers on leave, arrange temporary coverage, and face damages if they violate the law.

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid, so a worker who cannot afford a quarter-year without a paycheck may be unable to use the right the law grants [S2].

The law excludes employees at worksites with fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles, and workers with less than 12 months of service or 1,250 hours in the prior year, leaving many lower-wage and small-firm workers uncovered [S2].

Employers must hold jobs and keep paying health premiums for workers on leave, and can deny reinstatement to the highest-paid 10 percent of their workforce when it would cause substantial economic injury [S2].
Spouses who work for the same employer must share a single 12-week entitlement for births, adoptions, or care of a sick parent, cutting the combined time off in half [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The real value is job security: before this law, a worker who took time off for a birth or a cancer diagnosis could simply be replaced with no recourse. The law's honest weaknesses are that the leave is unpaid, which limits who can actually use it, and that the 50-employee threshold leaves out most small businesses and their workers. The employer cost is real but modest, mostly holding jobs open and paying health premiums for people already on the payroll, and it is the price of a guarantee workers in most other wealthy countries already had.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 265-163 on February 3, the Senate passed its own version 71-27 on February 4, the House accepted the Senate's changes the same day, and the President signed it on February 5, 1993, making it Public Law 103-3.

narrative.text: Introduced January 5, 1993 as the first House bill of the new Congress, it was referred to three committees and reported by two of them, Education and Labor and Post Office and Civil Service [S6].
The House passed it on February 3, 1993 by a recorded vote of 265-163 [S8].
An attempt by opponents to send the bill back to committee with instructions failed 175-253 before the final vote [S7].
The Senate passed it on February 4, 1993 by a vote of 71-27, substituting the language of its companion bill S. 5 with an amendment [S9].
The Senate version added a sense-of-Congress provision calling on the Secretary of Defense to review the military's policy on gay and lesbian service members and report by July 15, 1993 [S4].
The House agreed to the Senate amendment on February 4, 1993, and the bill was presented to the President and signed the next day, becoming Public Law 103-3 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working people came out ahead: millions of employees at covered workplaces gained a federal right to take leave for a birth, adoption, or serious illness without losing their job or health insurance. The employers and business groups that opposed the mandate did not get the exemptions they sought, beyond the small-employer carve-out already in the bill.

for.name: Rep. William D. Ford
for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and guided it through committee and to House passage.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on February 5, 1993.

for.name: 40 House Republicans and 16 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage in both chambers.

against.name: Rep. Harris Fawell
against.what_they_did: Moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions; the motion failed 175-253.

against.name: Business groups including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the leave mandate, arguing it imposed costs on employers, particularly small businesses.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic: 224 of 254 House Democrats and 55 of 57 Senate Democrats voted yes, compared with 40 of 175 House Republicans and 16 of 43 Senate Republicans.

industries.industry: Employers with 50 or more employees (private firms and public agencies)
industries.note: These employers must grant up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave, keep paying health premiums for workers on leave, and can face damages for violations [S2]. In exchange, their employees gain a guarantee of job and health coverage during family and medical emergencies.

industries.industry: Small employers (fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles)
industries.note: They are exempt from the mandate, saving them compliance costs, but their employees get no federal leave guarantee, so workers at small firms are left out of the protection [S2].
The law requires employers to maintain health benefits for workers on leave, keeping employees enrolled in employer-based coverage instead of dropping insurance during a family crisis [S2].
